The GAL-TAN framework identifies political orientation on a single axis. Individuals and texts are placed according to the degree to which their views align with either pole, as follows:

  - Individuals at the GAL (Green/Alternative/Libertarian) pole support expanded
    personal freedoms and social liberalisation, for example: access to abortion,
    same-sex marriage, environmental protection, and multiculturalism.

  - Individuals at the TAN (Traditional/Authoritarian/Nationalist) pole prioritise
    order, tradition, and stability, and believe that the state should treat the
    maintenance of national identity as a priority, for example: restrictive
    immigration policy, emphasis on law and order, defence of traditional social
    institutions, and national sovereignty over supranational authority.

A text occupies a position on this axis to the extent that it argues FROM these commitments, not to the extent that it mentions the associated topics:

  - Environmental or immigration policy discussed in administrative or fiscal
    terms does not by itself indicate a position.
  - Nuclear expansion argued for energy security is not GAL.
  - Faster asylum processing argued on humanitarian grounds is not TAN.

# Summary

This document outlines a comprehensive political platform focused on economic transformation, public service reform, and addressing social inequalities.

## Economic and Environmental Priorities

The manifesto centers on responding to climate change through a "Green Industrial Revolution" creating one million jobs. This includes transitioning to renewable energy, upgrading 27 million homes for energy efficiency, and targeting net-zero carbon emissions. Major public investments totaling £400 billion would fund infrastructure, with £250 billion specifically for green initiatives. Key utilities including energy, water, rail, and mail would be brought into public ownership.

Full-fibre broadband would be provided free to all households by 2030 through a new public service.

## Public Services

Healthcare would receive substantial funding increases, with commitments to end privatisation, abolish prescription charges, and provide free dental check-ups. Social care would be transformed through a National Care Service offering free personal care for older people.

Education reforms include a National Education Service providing cradle-to-grave learning, abolishing tuition fees, restoring maintenance grants, expanding childcare, and increasing school funding.

Police numbers would be increased to reverse previous cuts, while justice reforms would address prison overcrowding and restore legal aid.

## Workers and Social Security

Workers' rights would be substantially expanded, including a £10 minimum wage, ending zero-hours contracts, and introducing sectoral collective bargaining. Working hours would gradually reduce to 32 per week without pay loss. Employee ownership stakes in large companies would be mandated.

Social security reforms would replace existing benefit systems, end the benefit cap, and increase support for disabled people and carers.

## Housing

Housing policy includes building over one million social homes in a decade, introducing rent controls, and providing greater protections for renters. Homelessness would be targeted through increased funding and new housing programs.

## Democratic Reform

Constitutional changes would include replacing the upper legislative chamber, reducing the voting age to 16, and decentralising power to regions. A constitutional convention would examine broader political reforms.

# Summary of 2019 UK General Election Manifesto

This manifesto outlines policy commitments across several key areas, focusing on leaving the European Union and subsequent domestic priorities.

## Brexit
The central pledge is completing EU withdrawal by January, implementing a negotiated agreement that removes the UK from EU customs arrangements and single market rules. This would enable independent trade policy, border controls, and regulatory autonomy. The manifesto emphasises this as essential before other priorities can be addressed.

## Healthcare
Major NHS commitments include £34 billion additional annual funding, recruitment of 50,000 nurses and 6,000 doctors, 50 million extra GP appointments annually, and construction of 40 new hospitals. Mental health services would receive equal priority to physical health. A visa scheme would fast-track qualified overseas health workers. Social care would receive £1 billion annually, with cross-party work sought on long-term reform, guaranteeing nobody would need to sell their home for care costs.

## Education and Skills
Schools would receive £14 billion over three years, with minimum funding of £5,000 per secondary pupil and £4,000 per primary pupil. Teacher starting salaries would rise to £30,000. A £3 billion National Skills Fund would support adult retraining, alongside upgraded further education colleges and apprenticeship expansion.

## Public Safety
Twenty thousand additional police officers would be recruited. Sentencing for serious crimes would be toughened, automatic early release ended for serious offenders, and knife crime addressed through new court orders. Victim support legislation and domestic abuse measures feature prominently.

## Immigration
An Australian-style points-based system would replace freedom of movement, prioritising skilled workers with job offers. Five-year residency requirements would apply before accessing certain benefits. Settlement scheme protections continue for existing EU residents.

## Economic Policy
Commitments include no increases to income tax, VAT, or National Insurance rates, plus raising the National Insurance threshold. The National Living Wage would increase to £10.50 hourly. Business rates would be reviewed and reduced for retail. Borrowing rules limit investment to 3% of GDP while avoiding day-to-day deficit spending.

## Infrastructure
Major transport investments include Northern Powerhouse Rail, Midlands Rail Hub, and nationwide gigabit broadband by 2025. Electric vehicle charging networks would expand. Town regeneration funds would support local improvements.

## Environment
Net zero emissions by 2050 remains the target. Offshore wind capacity would reach 40GW by 2030. Tree planting would increase to 75,000 acres annually. Plastic waste exports to non-OECD countries would be banned. A fracking moratorium continues.

## Housing
Targets include 300,000 homes annually by mid-2020s. Long-term fixed-rate mortgages would reduce deposit requirements. Local discount schemes would prioritise first-time buyers. "No fault" evictions would be abolished for renters.

## Defence and Foreign Policy
Defence spending would exceed 2% of GDP with annual increases. Nuclear deterrent maintenance continues. Trade agreements targeting 80% coverage within three years are planned, including with the USA, Australia, and New Zealand. The 0.7% development aid commitment remains.
